title: Syntactic categories by distribution
summary: From zero: what a category is, the eleven categories on Dr. Nie's list with what each one does, the two kinds of test (endings and neighbors) that prove a label, and how to label every word of a sentence with a reason, the way HW 1 and the oral exam ask.
sourceNote: Week 2 handout (Syntactic categories), the diagnostic quiz, Carnie videos 2.1 to 2.2 (Parts of Speech), HW 1. Rebuilt for readers who missed class: each term is defined before it is used.

sections.heading: Start here: what a category is, and why meaning can't find it

blocks.body: A group of words that **behave the same way**: they take the same endings and show up in the same spots in a sentence. Noun, verb, adjective and so on. You may know them as 'parts of speech'.

blocks.md: **One example.** In *I walked around the park*, *walked* is a verb. In *I took three walks around the park*, *walks* is a noun. It's the same event, the same meaning. What changed is the **endings** (-ed vs plural -s) and the **neighbors** (after *I* vs after *three*). That's the whole idea of this chapter.

blocks.caption: Every word carries two 'ID cards': the endings it can take and the neighbors it can have. Same word 'walk', two sets of cards, two categories. Hover each card.

blocks.body: Where a word can show up. Dr. Nie splits it in two. **Morphological distribution**: which endings (affixes) it can take. **Syntactic distribution**: which words it can sit next to. A category is decided by distribution, never by meaning.

School says 'a noun is a person, place or thing'. It fails right away: *destruction* is an action, *happiness* is a feeling, and both are nouns (*the destruction*, *two happinesses*). On a test, 'it's a noun because it's a thing' earns nothing. 'It's a noun because it follows *the* and takes plural *-s*' earns full credit.

**Derivational** endings make a new word, often of a new category: *-tion* makes nouns (*isolat-ion*), *-ize* makes verbs (*real-ize*), *-able* makes adjectives (*read-able*). **Inflectional** endings just adjust a word and keep its category: plural *-s* on nouns, *-ed* / *-ing* on verbs, *-er* / *-est* on adjectives.

rows.label: As a test
rows.left: -ness at the end → it's a noun

blocks.caption: Both kinds of ending are evidence. If a word can take a noun ending, that's a reason to call it a noun.

blocks.prompt: *Quickly*: which ending does it have, is it derivational or inflectional, and what category does it make?
blocks.answer: *-ly*, derivational (it turns the adjective *quick* into a new word), and it makes an **adverb**.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this** Part-of-speech tagging, this exact labeling job done by a program, is step one of almost every language app. A voice assistant hearing 'Book me a flight' has to decide *book* is a verb before it can do anything. Taggers fail exactly where the tests in this chapter disagree.
blocks.label: world

sections.heading: The eleven categories, one at a time

blocks.md: Dr. Nie's list has eleven categories. Here is each one with what it **does** in plain words, a few examples from the handout, and one quick test. Don't memorize the examples; learn the job and the test.

rows: names a thing, person, idea, event
granola, party, joy, Jake, they, him, who
describes a verb, adjective, or the whole sentence
a little relation word before a noun phrase
on, of, by, into, with, to
followed by a noun phrase: *on the table*
comes first in a noun phrase: which one, how many, whose
the, a, this, every, two, his, which
introduces a whole clause inside a sentence
blocks.title: The eleven categories

blocks.body: **Lexical** categories (N, V, Adj, Adv) carry content, and new words join them all the time (*rage-bait*, *to google*), so they're called **open class**. **Functional** categories (P, D, C, Aux, Mod, T, Neg) carry grammar, and you basically can't invent new ones, so they're **closed class**.

right.title: Functional (closed class)
right.sub: P · D · C · Aux · Mod · T · Neg

blocks.caption: The practical difference: test the lexical words, look up the functional ones.

blocks.body: **Three words that fool everyone.** Pronouns (*they*, *him*) and question words used as nouns (*who*, *what*) are **N** on her list. Possessives (*his*, *our*) and numbers (*two*) are **D**. And *to* before a plain verb is **T**, not P: *to eat* is T, *to Paris* is P.

blocks.prompt: *Their* in *their new roof*: which category, and is it open or closed?
blocks.answer: **D** (determiner): possessives are determiners on her list. Closed class.

blocks.prompt: *To* in *I want to leave* vs *I went to Rome*?
blocks.answer: *to leave*: **T** (before a plain verb). *to Rome*: **P** (before a noun phrase).

sections.heading: The tests that prove a label

blocks.body: A sentence with one blank. Every word that fits the blank naturally belongs to the same category. *The ___ slept* finds nouns. *They will ___* finds verbs. *the ___ dog* finds adjectives.

rows: follows a subject; follows Aux / Mod / T ('will run', 'to run'); follows adverbs; can be negated with 'not'
follows determiners and adjectives ('the big __'); can be negated with 'no' ('no computers')
sits between D and N ('the __ dog'); follows degree adverbs ('very __')
CANNOT sit between D and N; follows degree adverbs ('very __')
blocks.slide: The test table: this is what you cite

blocks.md: **How to read that table.** Pick the row for the category you think it is. Show one ending from the middle column **or** one position from the right column. That's your proof. Two proofs is better than one.

blocks.caption: Her sharpest test, drawn. 'very' modifies both adjectives and adverbs, so it can't tell them apart: but only an adjective can stand between a determiner and its noun. 'The quick run' is fine; '*the quickly run' is out. When the quiz asks you to prove Adj vs Adv, this frame is the proof to cite. Hover any row.

blocks.body: *Very* does NOT separate adjectives from adverbs: *very quick* and *very quickly* both work. Use the **D ___ N** frame instead: *the quick run* ✓, '*the quickly run' ✗. Adjectives fit between a determiner and a noun; adverbs never do.

blocks.title: Labeling handout sentence (3), one word at a time

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: Handout sentence (3). Label each word and give a reason, left to right. Watch the list grow.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **That = D.** Test: on the closed list of determiners (the, a, this, that…); it comes before the adjectives and noun.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **extremely = Adv.** Test: ends in -ly; can't go between a determiner and a noun ('*the extremely alligator').

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **leathery = Adj.** Test: fits between D and N ('that leathery alligator') and takes 'very'.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **alligator = N.** Test: follows D + Adj; takes plural -s ('alligators').

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **greatly = Adv.** Test: ends in -ly and describes the verb 'hopes'.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **hopes = V.** Test: has the -s ending for 'he/she/it'; follows the subject; negates as 'does not hope'.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **to = T.** Test: 'to' right before a plain verb is the infinitive marker T, not a preposition.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **be = Aux.** Test: a helper verb: be, have, do are auxiliaries.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **eating = V.** Test: -ing ending; comes after the auxiliary 'be'.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **us = N.** Test: a pronoun, and on Dr. Nie's list pronouns count as nouns.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **for = P.** Test: a preposition: closed class, followed by a noun phrase.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **dinner = N.** Test: follows the preposition; plural 'dinners' works.

lines: That extremely leathery alligator greatly hopes to be eating us for dinner tonight.
frames.caption: **tonight = Adv.** Test: a time word that describes when; can't sit between D and N.

blocks.prompt: Prove that *fast* in *a fast car* is an adjective, not an adverb.
blocks.answer: It fits the D ___ N frame (*a fast car*) and takes *-er* (*a faster car*). An adverb can't sit between *a* and *car*.

blocks.prompt: Prove *arrival* is a noun with an ending test and a neighbor test.
blocks.answer: Ending: *-al* here is a noun-making ending, and it takes plural *-s* (*arrivals*). Neighbor: it fits after *the* (*the arrival was late*).

sections.heading: Grammatical properties: what categories carry in any language

blocks.md: The tests above are for English. The second half of the handout lists **properties** categories tend to carry in every language, so you can spot a verb in Zulu or a noun in Japanese on the homework. Two groups: what **verbs** carry, and what **nouns** carry.

blocks.body: How many participants a verb **needs**. Intransitive = 1 (*Ming sneezed*), transitive = 2 (*Sarah helped Ming*), ditransitive = 3 (*Taro gave the child a book*).

cards.title: Tense
lines: When it happened: past, present, future.

cards.title: Agreement
lines: The verb copies a feature of a noun.

blocks.caption: Properties verbs carry. Zulu shows agreement dramatically: *aba-ntu ba-bona um-fana*, 'the people see the boy', where *ba-* on the verb agrees with 'people'.

cards.title: Number
lines: singular, plural; Hebrew even has a dual: *yomáyim* 'two days'

cards.title: Gender / noun class
lines: A grammatical group, not always about sex.

cards.title: Case
lines: The noun's job, marked on the noun.

blocks.caption: Properties nouns carry. Because Japanese marks case, *Hanako-ga Taro-o* and *Taro-o Hanako-ga* mean the same thing: Hanako hit Taro.

blocks.md: **Adjectives and adverbs have properties too.** Adjectives can be **attributive** (*a fast car*, before the noun) or **predicative** (*the car is fast*, after *be*); they can **agree** (French *vin blanc* / *porte blanche*); they have **comparative / superlative** forms (*heavier* / *heaviest*). Adverbs come in types: manner (*slowly*), frequency (*often*), time (*yesterday*), degree (*very*), modal (*possibly*).

blocks.body: **Arabic for the oral exam** Arabic shows nearly every property on the handout in one sentence: *al-bint-u l-ṣaġīr-at-u qaraʔ-at kitāb-a-hā* ('the little girl read her book'). Definiteness (*al-*), gender agreement on the adjective (*-at*), case (*-u* NOM, *-a* ACC), verb agreement (*-at* 3SG.F), a possessive clitic (*=hā*). Bring one glossed Arabic sentence and you can demonstrate five properties in a minute.

blocks.title: Maurice very slowly dried the dishes with some worn red towels.
blocks.body:
Label every word; justify the hard ones.

1. Maurice N (proper noun; takes possessive 's) · very Adv (degree) · slowly Adv (-ly; *'the slowly dishes') · dried V (-ed; follows the subject) · the D · dishes N (plural -s; follows D) · with P · some D · worn Adj (between D and N; 'very worn') · red Adj (between D and N; 'redder') · towels N (plural; follows D + Adj + Adj).
2. The diagnostic's Q2 asked for three multi-word constituents: 'the dishes', 'some worn red towels', 'with some worn red towels'. Why those count is Week 5's topic.

blocks.prompt: Handout (24): 'My anxious neighbors have just told me that their new roof caught on fire.' Label the functional categories.
blocks.answer: My D · have Aux · that C · their D · on P. (just is Adv; anxious, new Adj; neighbors, me, roof, fire N; told, caught V.)

blocks.prompt: Handout (23): 'Every professor likely knows that students prefer to have shorter assignments.' What are 'likely', 'to', and 'shorter', with a test each?
blocks.answer: likely = Adv (modal adverb; *'the likely professor' in this sense fails the D__N frame as an adverb: note 'likely' can also be an Adj elsewhere; here it modifies 'knows'). to = T (infinitive marker before bare 'have'). shorter = Adj (comparative -er; sits between D and N: 'the shorter assignments').

blocks.prompt: 'Book' in 'Book me a flight' vs 'the book with the yellow cover'. Same category?
blocks.answer: No. First: V: follows nothing but takes an object, can be negated ('don't book'), takes -ed. Second: N: follows D, takes plural. Same form, two categories, decided by distribution. (This is also Ling 115's POS-tagging example.)

rows: A group of words that take the same endings and fit the same spots.
Where a word can appear: its endings (morphological) and neighbors (syntactic).
Makes a new word, often a new category (-ness, -ize, -able).
A sentence with a blank; whatever fits shares a category.
N, V, Adj, Adv: content words, new ones added all the time.
P, D, C, Aux, Mod, T, Neg: grammar words, a fixed list.
the, a, this, every, his, two: starts a noun phrase.
that, if, whether: introduces a clause inside a sentence.
How many participants a verb needs (1, 2 or 3).
When it happened / whether it's ongoing or finished.
A verb (or adjective) copying a feature of a noun.
Adjective before a noun (a fast car) / after be (the car is fast).
blocks.title: Words from this chapter

exercises.title: Label every word, and prove three of them
exercises.prompt: 'The exhausted students will probably finish their difficult assignments before midnight.' Label each word with one of the eleven categories. Then, for *exhausted*, *probably*, and *before*, give one test each that proves the label.
hints: Go word by word with the frames from the chapter: can it follow 'the'? take -s or -ed? take -er/-est or 'very'? sit between a determiner and a noun? take an NP after it?

The traps: *exhausted* looks like a verb (-ed) but here it sits between D and N and takes 'very': that's the adjective frame. *probably* modifies the verb and can't be 'very probably… the probably student': adverb. And 'will' is an auxiliary, not a verb.
A test is only a proof if you show it *passes* here and would *fail* for the competing category. 'very exhausted' ✓ (Adj), '✱very finish' ✗ (V).
solution: The D · exhausted Adj · students N · will Aux · probably Adv · finish V · their D · difficult Adj · assignments N · before P · midnight N.
*exhausted* = Adj: fits D __ N ('the exhausted students'), takes 'very' ('very exhausted'), and can be predicative ('the students are exhausted'). As a verb it couldn't take 'very'.
*probably* = Adv: modifies the verb/sentence, moves freely ('Probably the students will…'), and can't fit D __ N ('✱the probably students').
*before* = P here: it takes an NP complement ('before midnight') and the phrase answers 'when?'. (Note: 'before' can also be a C: 'before they left': the complement decides.)
exercises.why: POS tagging (LING 115) is this exercise done a million times by a program, and the program's errors are exactly the cases where the tests conflict: 'exhausted', 'before', 'that'. Knowing the tests is knowing where the machine will fail.

exercises.title: Same word, different category
exercises.prompt: For each pair, say the category of the italic word in each sentence and the one test that separates them: (a) 'She will *run* tomorrow' / 'She went for a *run*'. (b) '*That* book is mine' / 'I know *that* she left'. (c) 'He walked *fast*' / 'a *fast* car'.
hints: Don't look at the word: look at what's around it. What precedes it? What follows it? Can you add a plural, a past tense, 'very', 'the'?
The mistake is answering from the dictionary ('run is a verb'). Categories are positions, not words. 'a run' after a determiner, taking a plural ('runs'), is a noun.
For (b): a determiner 'that' sits before a noun and can be swapped for 'this'; a complementizer 'that' introduces a whole clause and can often be dropped ('I know she left').
solution: (a) V / N. Test: 'a run' follows a determiner and pluralizes ('two runs'); 'will run' follows an auxiliary and takes tense ('ran').
(b) D / C. Test: D 'that' swaps with 'this' and precedes a noun; C 'that' precedes a full clause with its own subject and verb and can be omitted.

(c) Adv / Adj. Test: 'a fast car' fits D __ N and takes 'very'/'faster'; 'walked fast' modifies the verb and can't fit D __ N ('✱a fast'). English 'fast' happens to have the same form in both categories: most adverbs would show -ly.
exercises.why: Every ambiguity in a headline ('Police help dog bite victim') and every failure of autocorrect comes from a word that lives in two categories. Resolving it by distribution: not by memory: is the skill.

exercises.title: Which frame decides it?
exercises.prompt: You need to prove *careful* is an adjective and not an adverb. Which frame settles it?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **the ___ driver.** *The careful driver* works; an adverb would not fit.
exercises.why: Picking the one frame that separates the two candidates is exactly what the quiz grades.

choices.feedback: Yes: only adjectives fit between a determiner and a noun.
Both adjectives and adverbs take 'very', so it can't decide.
That frame finds adverbs; 'careful' fails it, which is a hint but not the positive proof.
Adding -ly makes a different word (carefully).

exercises.title: What is 'to' here?
exercises.prompt: *She decided to stay.* What category is *to*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **T.** It sits right before the plain verb *stay*.
exercises.why: One of the three traps on her list.

choices.feedback: Yes: 'to' before a plain verb is T.
A preposition 'to' comes before a noun phrase (to Rome).
C is that, if, whether.
It isn't describing anything.

exercises.title: What is 'his'?
exercises.prompt: *His old car broke down.* What category is *his*?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **D.** Swap it for *the*: *The old car broke down.* Same slot.
exercises.why: Swapping with 'the' is a fast way to prove D.

choices.feedback: Yes: possessives are determiners on her list.
Pronouns like 'him' are N, but possessive 'his' fills the D slot (compare 'the old car').
It doesn't take 'very' or fit between D and N.
It isn't followed by a noun phrase as a relation word.

exercises.title: Count the participants
exercises.prompt: *The waiter handed me the bill.* What is the verb's valency?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
exercises.why: Valency comes back in Week 8 as theta roles.

choices.feedback: Yes: the waiter, me, the bill.
There's a third participant: the one who receives the bill.
More than one participant is needed.
Only three participants are involved.

exercises.title: Which kind of ending?
exercises.prompt: *teach* → *teacher*. What kind of ending is *-er* here?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: **Derivational.** It turns the verb *teach* into the noun *teacher*.
exercises.why: Same-looking endings can be different morphemes; the category of the root tells you which.

choices.text: Derivational: it makes a new noun
choices.feedback: Yes: a verb became a noun, so it's derivational.
Comparative -er goes on adjectives (tall-er); teach isn't an adjective.
Plural is -s.
It is a suffix: teach + -er.
